title: Election Simulator: Campaign to Victory
theme: Indian Democratic Process, Campaign Strategy & Civic Education
description: You are a Class 11 student at Sardar Patel Vidyalaya, running for Student Council President. Your school election mirrors the great Indian democratic tradition -- from filing nominations to election day. Navigate debates, alliances, scandals, media, and rallies across 10 intense rounds. Manage your voter support, campaign funds in INR, credibility, team morale, media coverage, and public trust. Will you win with integrity, or will the pressure of politics change who you are? Every choice teaches you something real about how India's democracy works.
learning_objectives: Understand the Indian democratic process and the role of the Election Commission of India (ECI)
Learn about the Model Code of Conduct and ethical campaigning practices
Develop strategic thinking through campaign budget management in INR
Build media literacy to handle misinformation, rumours, and responsible reporting
Understand coalition politics, alliance-building, and the art of compromise
Learn about NOTA, voter turnout, electoral integrity, and the importance of every vote
Practise crisis management and reputation repair under pressure
Recognise the parallels between student elections and real Indian general elections

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: You are running for Student Council President at Sardar Patel Vidyalaya -- a prestigious school with 1,200 students
Each round presents a campaign scenario inspired by real Indian democratic processes
Pick one of the available options -- every choice changes your Voter Support, Campaign Funds, Credibility, Team Morale, Media Coverage, and Public Trust
Manage your campaign budget in INR wisely: spending big on posters and chai stalls may boost support but drain your funds
Navigate 10 rounds covering announcements, debates, alliances, scandals, media strategy, and election day
Compete against your main rival Rohit Malhotra, who has deep pockets and family connections
Learn real facts about Indian elections, the ECI, NOTA, Model Code of Conduct, and more as you play
tips: There is no single winning strategy -- every choice has trade-offs, just like real politics
Credibility and Public Trust are hard to build and easy to lose -- protect them
Watch your Campaign Funds -- you cannot spend what you do not have, and overspending invites scrutiny
Team Morale affects how effectively your volunteers campaign in later rounds
Media Coverage can be a double-edged sword -- high visibility means high scrutiny
Just like in real Indian elections, alliances can multiply your strength but also create obligations

psychological_skills: Media literacy and critical evaluation of information

player_profile.name: Student Council President Candidate
player_profile.goal: Win the Student Council President election at Sardar Patel Vidyalaya through smart campaigning and ethical leadership
player_profile.background: A Class 11 student known for being sincere, hardworking, and well-liked by juniors and seniors alike. You have served on the school's cultural committee for two years. Your campaign manager Priya convinced you to run after the previous council failed to deliver on its promises. You are the underdog going up against Rohit Malhotra, whose family is wealthy and well-connected. Your weapon is authenticity. Your challenge is making it count.

competitors.name: Rohit Malhotra
competitors.description: Son of a prominent industrialist and school trustee board member. Rohit has unlimited campaign funds, a professional PR team, and connections that go all the way to the school management. He is charming, well-dressed, and throws the best parties. But many students feel he is out of touch with their real problems -- he has never eaten in the school canteen or used the common washrooms. His campaign slogan is 'Modernise. Upgrade. Win.' He represents the establishment.

npcs.name: Priya Menon
npcs.description: Your best friend and the sharpest strategist in school. Priya runs the quiz club, maintains colour-coded spreadsheets for everything, and has read every book on Indian political history. She is brutally honest, fiercely loyal, and keeps you grounded when the campaign madness gets overwhelming.

npcs.name: Ankit Verma
npcs.description: Editor of 'The Patel Post', the school newspaper with an Instagram page that reaches every student. Ankit models himself on real investigative journalists. He is sharp, neutral, and prides himself on never taking sides. His endorsement or criticism can swing the election overnight.

npcs.name: Dr. Sharma
npcs.description: The Political Science teacher who oversees the school election process. She designed the election rules based on actual Election Commission of India guidelines. Strict but fair, she has disqualified candidates in the past for violating the school's Model Code of Conduct. She believes student elections should teach real democratic values.

npcs.name: Rohit Malhotra
npcs.description: Wealthy, connected, and polished. Rohit sees the election as his birthright. He has a professional PR consultant, printed merchandise, and the backing of the school's elite circle. Underestimating him would be a mistake.

npc_dialogues.text: Listen, we have Rs 50,000 and a lot of heart. Rohit just ordered 500 printed T-shirts with his face on them. We cannot outspend him, so we have to out-think him. First impressions matter -- how we announce your candidacy sets the tone for everything.

I am covering all candidates equally for The Patel Post. Give me something real to write about -- not slogans, not promises. The students are tired of empty words. Show me substance and I will give you fair coverage.

Remember, our school election follows the Model Code of Conduct -- just like real Indian elections. No personal attacks, no bribing voters with gifts, no misuse of school property. The Election Commission of India was established to ensure free and fair elections, and I intend to uphold those same standards here.

I heard you are putting together a team. Cute. My PR consultant handled the municipal corporation elections last year. This school election is a stepping stone for me. Do not take it personally when you lose.

The debate is tomorrow and 800 students will be watching. I have prepared a dossier on every issue -- fee hike, canteen quality, sports facilities, hostel conditions. The key is to be specific. Anyone can say 'I will improve things.' Tell them HOW.

The debate is where elections are won and lost. Did you know that in the 2014 Indian general elections, the BJP's focus on development over dynasty politics completely shifted the narrative? Substance beats style in the long run.

I want every candidate to submit a detailed expenditure report. In real Indian elections, the Election Commission sets spending limits -- Rs 95 lakh for a Lok Sabha seat, Rs 40 lakh for a Vidhan Sabha seat. Transparency in funding is the backbone of democratic integrity.

This rumour about you is clearly fabricated. We need to respond, but HOW we respond matters more than WHAT we say. Remember, in politics, an unanswered allegation becomes accepted truth. But a panicked response looks guilty. We need calm, factual, decisive action.
Oh, those rumours? I have no idea where they came from. Politics is a rough game, my friend. If you cannot handle a little heat, maybe student leadership is not for you.

Coalition politics is fascinating. Did you know that in Indian general elections, coalition governments ruled from 1989 to 2014? The United Front, NDA, UPA -- every alliance required compromise. The question is always: what are you willing to give up to gain power?

Ground campaigning is the oldest form of democratic engagement. Even with social media, nothing replaces meeting voters face to face. In Indian elections, candidates still do padyatras -- walking tours through constituencies. The personal touch builds trust no advertisement can match.

Rohit's Instagram page has 3,000 followers because he ran paid ads. Our school newspaper coverage is organic and trusted. Remember, in the 2020 Delhi elections, ground-level WhatsApp campaigns were more effective than million-rupee TV ads. Authentic messaging wins.

Your final rally speech will be published in full on The Patel Post. This is your closing argument. In real Indian elections, the final rally before the silent period is often the most memorable. Vajpayee, Modi, Indira Gandhi -- they all understood the power of a closing speech. Make yours count.

Today is election day. The Model Code of Conduct prohibits campaigning within 100 metres of the polling booth. No distributing pamphlets, no offering refreshments to voters, no last-minute promises. Any violation will be treated as it would by the real ECI -- seriously.

This is it. Every handshake, every speech, every late-night poster session -- it all comes down to today. Our polling booth agents are in place. The NOTA option is on the ballot, just like in real elections since 2013. Let democracy speak.

rounds.title: Round 1: Announcing Your Candidacy
rounds.story:
The school assembly hall is buzzing. Dr. Sharma steps up to the microphone and announces the Student Council elections for the new academic year at Sardar Patel Vidyalaya.

'Nominations are open. Any student from Class 9 to 12 may file their candidacy,' she declares. 'This election will follow the Model Code of Conduct, just as the Election Commission of India mandates for real elections.'

Rohit Malhotra is already shaking hands in the front row, his team distributing glossy printed pamphlets. His father donated the new auditorium last year.

Priya slides into the seat next to you. 'We need to make our announcement count. Rohit has money and connections. We have authenticity. How do we launch this?'

She hands you four ideas she brainstormed last night.

Your campaign funds: Rs {{campaign_funds}}
Your credibility: {{credibility}}%
rounds.goal: Make a strong first impression and establish your campaign identity
rounds.setting: School assembly hall, Day 1 of election season

npc_dialogue.text: Rohit just ordered 500 printed T-shirts. We cannot outspend him. We have to out-think him. First impressions set the entire narrative.
In India, filing your nomination is the first step. The ECI verifies every candidate's eligibility. Here, I verify yours. Good luck.

choices.label: Go Viral: Social Media Blitz
choices.description: Get your tech-savvy friends to create fire Instagram reels, memes with trending audio, and flood every WhatsApp group. A campaign reel showing real school problems -- broken water coolers, canteen food, crumbling sports equipment -- with the tagline 'Enough Talk, Time for Change.' Costs money for production and QR code printing.
choices.feedback:
Your campaign reel goes semi-viral in school -- the meme comparing canteen food to hospital food gets 600 shares on Instagram within hours. Students are laughing, tagging friends, and suddenly everyone knows your name. But Ankit from The Patel Post writes a pointed piece: 'Memes are not manifestos. Where is the policy substance?' Dr. Sharma privately notes that viral content without substance is a pattern she has seen in real Indian elections too. High visibility achieved, but you have built attention without yet building trust.

Did you know? In Indian elections, social media spending has exploded -- the BJP and Congress together spent over Rs 100 crore on digital ads during the 2019 general elections. The Election Commission now requires parties to report digital spending.

choices.label: Traditional Assembly Speech
choices.description: Request 5 minutes during morning assembly. Stand at the podium and deliver a powerful speech about the real issues students face -- fee hikes, poor canteen food, lack of mental health support. No gimmicks, no memes, just your voice and conviction. The old-fashioned way.
choices.feedback:
You stand at the podium and speak from the heart. You mention the Class 9 students whose water cooler has been broken for three months. You mention the hostel students who eat the same dal every night. You mention the Class 12 students who have no counsellor during board exam season. The hall is quiet. Then, slowly, applause builds from the back rows -- the juniors, the hostel students, the ones who usually do not participate. Ankit writes: 'One candidate remembered that speeches are supposed to be about the audience, not the speaker.' You did not go viral, but you planted a seed of respect.

Did you know? In India's Parliament, the tradition of powerful oratory dates back to Jawaharlal Nehru's 'Tryst with Destiny' speech in 1947. Great democracies are built on the power of authentic public speaking.

choices.label: Door-to-Door Hostel Campaign
choices.description: Skip the big stage. Spend the first three days personally visiting every hostel wing, every classroom during breaks, and every sports ground. Introduce yourself, listen to what students actually want, and take notes. Slow but genuine. This is the padyatra of school politics.
choices.feedback:
You spend three days walking into hostel rooms, sitting in the canteen during dinner, and chatting with students on the football field. The Class 9 students are surprised that a senior even knows their names. The hostel students open up about the food, the broken ceiling fans, the 10 PM curfew that makes no sense during exam season. Priya tracks every concern in her spreadsheet. Rohit's team laughs: 'They are doing door-to-door? How cute.' But by Friday, corridors are buzzing: 'That candidate actually came and talked to us.' You are building something real.

Did you know? The Indian tradition of 'jan sampark' (public contact) campaigns and padyatras goes back to Mahatma Gandhi's Dandi March. Even in modern elections, candidates who do ground-level campaigning consistently outperform those who rely only on media.

choices.label: Celebrity Endorsement Attempt
choices.description: Your cousin knows a local YouTuber with 200K subscribers who graduated from this school. Get them to post a story endorsing you. Borrow some celebrity shine. Also get the school cricket captain and head of the drama club to publicly back you on Day 1. Big names, big splash.
choices.feedback:
The YouTuber posts a story: 'My school's next president should be...' and tags you. For 24 hours, you are the most talked-about person in school. The cricket captain poses with you for a photo that gets 400 likes. But the glow fades fast. Students start asking: 'Why does a YouTuber care about our canteen food?' Ankit writes a scathing piece: 'Celebrity endorsements -- borrowed fame or earned respect?' Dr. Sharma privately tells Priya: 'In real Indian elections, celebrity campaigning is common but rarely decisive. Voters ultimately care about issues, not star power.' You got attention, but not the kind that lasts.

Did you know? Indian political parties regularly use Bollywood stars for campaigning. However, research shows that celebrity endorsements have declining impact -- voters increasingly value candidate credibility over star power.

rounds.image_prompt: a vibrant school assembly hall filled with excited students, colorful banners hanging, a microphone on stage, and a spotlight illuminating Dr. Sharma as she speaks, pamphlets fluttering in hand.
rounds.coaching_moment: How you announce your candidacy sets the register for your entire campaign. In Indian school elections, as in national ones, first impressions are about authenticity — voters are immediately sorting candidates into 'like me' or 'different from me.' The medium you choose signals your values before you say a word.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What tradeoff did this decision reveal? What did you gain, and what did you give up?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Round 2: Building Your Team
rounds.story:
One week into the campaign. Priya has been working 16-hour days, but she cannot run the entire operation alone. You need a team.

Three groups have approached you, each offering to join -- but each comes with conditions.

First: the Sports Wing crew -- Arjun the cricket captain and his athlete friends. Popular, loud, and they can pack any rally. But Arjun wants the Vice-President slot, and he has a reputation for being aggressive with juniors.

Second: the Academic Council -- led by Sneha, the school topper. Respected, articulate, and great at research. But they want a written promise that the council will prioritise academics over sports and cultural events.

Third: a mixed group of enthusiastic Class 9 and 10 students. No connections, no reputation, but genuine belief in your message. They will work for nothing except the chance to be part of something real.

Priya says: 'We can only absorb one main group right now. Who do we bring in?'

Meanwhile, Rohit has hired an actual event management firm to run his campaign.

Your team morale: {{team_morale}}%
Your campaign funds: Rs {{campaign_funds}}
rounds.goal: Build your campaign team -- every alliance has trade-offs
rounds.setting: School canteen, strategy meeting over chai and samosas

npc_dialogue.text: In coalition politics, every ally brings strength and baggage. Choose wisely. We need people who believe in the cause, not just people who want to be on the winning side.
I see you are recruiting. Cute. My event management team handled the BJP youth wing rally in Lucknow last month. But sure, your Class 9 volunteers with crayons are adorable.

choices.label: Recruit the Sports Wing (Arjun's Athletes)
choices.description: Arjun's crew brings raw popularity and physical energy. They can fill a rally hall in minutes and their chants echo through the corridors. But making Arjun VP means associating with his aggressive reputation. Some junior students are intimidated by him.
choices.feedback:
Arjun's crew hits the ground running. Within two days, your campaign posters cover every corridor and your rally attendance triples. The sports wing is firmly behind you. But a Class 9 student quietly tells Priya: 'Arjun pushed my friend during inter-house cricket. If he is your VP, I am not voting for you.' Word spreads. Ankit writes: 'A leader is known by the company they keep.' The strength Arjun brings casts a shadow over your campaign's character.

Did you know? In Indian politics, alliance partners often bring electoral strength but also controversies. The coalition dharma requires balancing power with principles -- a challenge every Indian PM from V.P. Singh to Manmohan Singh has faced.

choices.label: Recruit the Academic Council (Sneha's Group)
choices.description: Sneha's group adds intellectual credibility. They will demolish opponents in debates and draft bulletproof policy documents. But their demand to prioritise academics over sports and culture will alienate athletes and artists.
choices.feedback:
Sneha's team rewrites your manifesto with actual data -- survey results showing 72% of students want extended library hours and better lab equipment. Your debate preparation improves dramatically. But when word gets out that sports funding might be cut, the basketball team revolts. The band members confront you at lunch: 'So the toppers are running the show now?' You gain the intellectual high ground but lose the creative and athletic communities.

Did you know? In India, the Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog) often had to balance development priorities across sectors. Resource allocation is the central challenge of governance -- whether in a school council or the Union Budget.

choices.label: Recruit the Enthusiastic Juniors (Class 9-10)
choices.description: Young, unknown, and without political capital. But genuine, energetic, and free of hidden agendas. Building from the bottom up is slower but creates a movement, not just a campaign. This is how grassroots democracy works.
choices.feedback:
Your new volunteers are a breath of fresh air. They make hand-painted posters in the art room, personally invite classmates, and bring infectious energy. Priya trains them efficiently. A photo of your junior volunteers making posters with watercolours goes viral on the school Instagram. Caption: 'This is what a real campaign looks like.' Rohit's team privately admits they are jealous of your volunteer energy. The juniors represent the largest voting bloc in school -- and they are now personally invested in your success.

Did you know? In Indian elections, booth-level workers and grassroots volunteers are the backbone of every successful campaign. The BJP's systematic booth-level management strategy has been credited as a key factor in their electoral successes since 2014.

choices.label: Recruit All Three Groups (Ambitious Coalition)
choices.description: Why choose? Invite everyone and manage the coalition. More people, more power. But managing conflicting egos and demands could be a nightmare. Priya warns: 'This could blow up spectacularly.'
choices.feedback:
Day one is electric. Day two, Arjun and Sneha clash over poster design. Day three, the juniors feel ignored. Day four, Arjun threatens to walk out because Sneha called his slogan 'juvenile.' Priya is running from crisis to crisis. Your funds drain on chai meetings and damage control. Rohit observes and smirks: 'My opponent cannot manage a team of 30. How will they manage a school of 1,200?' The painful lesson: trying to please everyone often pleases no one.

Did you know? India has experienced several coalition governments where managing diverse allies proved extremely difficult. The United Front government of 1996-98 collapsed partly because of internal contradictions. Coalition management is one of the hardest skills in politics.

Third: the Arts Collective, vibrant and creative, with passionate performers ready to energize events. They seek a platform for artistic expression but require the campaign to include their voices in decision-making.

rounds.coaching_moment: Coalition-building starts before the campaign, not during it. Each bloc you recruit brings votes but also obligations — their priorities become your priorities. The most dangerous coalition is one where you've made promises to groups with contradictory demands. Choose your team knowing you'll have to govern them, not just campaign with them.

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: Round 3: The First Debate
rounds.story:
The school auditorium is packed. All 1,200 students, from Class 9 to 12, are seated. Faculty lines the back row. Dr. Sharma herself is in the front, arms folded.

Ankit Verma is moderating the debate. The format: opening statements, three audience questions, and closing remarks.

Rohit goes first. Slick PowerPoint, professional graphics, his '5-Point Modernisation Plan' -- new AC in every classroom, a swimming pool, international exchange programmes. Students cheer.

Now it is your turn. Priya squeezes your hand backstage. 'They have glitter. You have substance.'

The first audience question comes from a Class 12 hostel student: 'The last three presidents promised to fix the canteen food and nothing changed. The fee was hiked by 15% this year with no improvements. Why should we trust anyone?'

1,200 faces stare at you.

Your credibility: {{credibility}}%
Your voter support: {{voter_support}}%
Your media coverage: {{media_coverage}}%
rounds.goal: Survive the debate and establish yourself as a serious candidate

npc_dialogue.text: I will ask tough questions. Do not take it personally. The students deserve answers, not performance. In a democracy, the press holds candidates accountable.
Be specific. Anyone can say 'I will improve things.' Tell them HOW and by WHEN. Specificity is credibility.

choices.label: Be Brutally Honest About Limitations
choices.description: Admit what a Student Council President can and cannot do. Explain that you cannot install ACs or build swimming pools -- those decisions are made by the school trust. Promise only what is in your power: a formal Student Grievance Cell, regular town halls, and a transparent budget report. Honesty over hype.
choices.feedback:
You grip the podium and say: 'I am not going to lie to you. The Student Council President cannot install air conditioning. That costs crores and is decided by the school trust. What I CAN do is create a Student Grievance Cell that gives our complaints actual weight. I CAN publish a monthly transparency report showing exactly how council funds are spent. No magic. Just real work.' The hall is quiet. Then a slow clap builds from the back. Ankit writes: 'First honest answer all day.' Rohit shifts uncomfortably. Dr. Sharma nods. You did not get the loudest applause, but you earned the deepest respect.

Did you know? In Indian elections, candidates routinely promise things beyond their constitutional power. The Election Commission has proposed rules against 'irrational promises' in manifestos. Honest campaigning is rare -- which is exactly why it stands out.

choices.label: Go on the Offensive Against Rohit
choices.description: Point out that Rohit's father sits on the school trust that approved the 15% fee hike. Ask publicly: 'Will you serve students or donors?' Facts, not personal attacks -- but the heat will be felt. Sometimes the best defence is a sharp offence.
choices.feedback:
You turn to Rohit: 'You promise to modernise the school. But your father sits on the school trust board that raised our fees by 15% without improving a single facility. Will the Student Council President serve students, or serve the trust?' The auditorium explodes. Rohit turns red. Students are on their feet. You dominated the moment. But afterwards, Priya pulls you aside: 'Effective, but dangerous. Ankit is writing that you went negative. And Rohit's supporters are furious. We made enemies today.' The offensive worked, but the cost is not fully visible yet.

Did you know? Negative campaigning is a staple of Indian elections. However, the Model Code of Conduct prohibits personal attacks based on caste, religion, or community. The line between legitimate criticism and mudslinging is one that real politicians struggle with constantly.

choices.label: Share a Personal Story That Connects
choices.description: Tell the story of your friend who had a panic attack before board exams and there was no support system available. Make it personal, emotional, and deeply real. Connect your candidacy to lived experience. Vulnerability can be the strongest weapon.
choices.feedback:
You grip the podium and say: 'Last year, my friend had a panic attack before the boards. There was no counsellor. No one to talk to. She sat in the washroom crying alone for an hour.' The hall goes completely silent. 'I am running because I do not want any student in this school to feel alone like that. My first action will be a peer support helpline -- students helping students.' A girl in the third row wipes her eyes. Even Rohit looks moved. Ankit writes: 'The debate has a clear emotional winner.' Your vulnerability became your greatest strength.

Did you know? In Indian democracy, some of the most powerful political moments have been personal. B.R. Ambedkar's own experience of caste discrimination drove his drafting of the Constitution. Personal stories have always been at the heart of political change in India.

choices.label: Present a Detailed Canteen Reform Plan
choices.description: Come prepared with a specific, costed, step-by-step plan to fix the canteen. You surveyed 200 students, got quotes from three caterers, and have a timeline. Turn the debate into a policy presentation. Boring? Maybe. Convincing? Absolutely.
choices.feedback:
You pull out a printed report: '200 students surveyed. 87% rate canteen food as poor. I obtained quotes from three caterers. A better meal plan costs only Rs 15 more per student per month. Here is the proposal I will submit to the school trust on Day 1.' The auditorium is quiet -- but it is the silence of respect. Dr. Sharma leans forward. 'This is the most prepared candidate I have seen in 15 years,' she tells a colleague. Rohit has no data to counter your numbers. Ankit's headline: 'One Candidate Brought Receipts.' You may not have won the crowd's heart, but you won their heads.

Did you know? In India, the Right to Information (RTI) Act of 2005 empowered citizens to demand transparency from the government. Your data-driven approach mirrors how RTI activists have transformed Indian governance by replacing rhetoric with evidence.

rounds.image_prompt: a bustling school auditorium filled with excited students, colorful banners hanging from the ceiling, a spotlight on the stage where a vibrant PowerPoint presentation is displayed, faculty watching intently
rounds.coaching_moment: Voters remember how you made them feel in a debate, not what you promised. Rohit Malhotra's money can buy posters but not authenticity. The debate is your equalizer — but only if you know which version of yourself to bring. Aggression energizes your base but alienates undecideds; vulnerability can flip a room if it's real.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why did you choose this option? What were you trying to protect or grow?

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Round 4: Campaign Fund Management
rounds.story:
Campaign week three. You sit in the canteen with Priya, staring at her budget spreadsheet.

'Here is the situation,' Priya says. 'We have Rs {{campaign_funds}} left. The election is in three weeks. We need to allocate this across four categories:'

1. Posters & Banners -- printed materials for corridors, classrooms, and the main gate
2. Digital Campaign -- Instagram ads, WhatsApp content creation, and video production
3. Events & Rallies -- sound system, stage decoration, and refreshments for campaign events
4. Chai Stalls & Ground Game -- tea and biscuits during hostel visits, canteen meetups, and personal outreach materials

'We cannot fund all four equally. We need to bet on one primary channel,' Priya says. 'What is our main spend?'

Meanwhile, Rohit is spending lavishly on everything -- his father's company is clearly funding the campaign, though nobody can prove it.

Dr. Sharma announces: 'All candidates must submit expense reports. The spending cap is Rs 75,000 per candidate -- mirroring how the ECI sets limits for real elections.'

Your campaign funds: Rs {{campaign_funds}}
Your media coverage: {{media_coverage}}%
rounds.goal: Allocate your limited budget strategically across campaign channels
rounds.setting: School canteen, Priya's laptop showing the budget spreadsheet

npc_dialogue.text: The ECI sets spending limits for every election. Rs 95 lakh for Lok Sabha, Rs 40 lakh for Vidhan Sabha. Candidates who exceed limits face disqualification. I am applying the same principle here.
I will be publishing every candidate's expense report in The Patel Post. Transparency in campaign financing is non-negotiable. The voters deserve to know where the money comes from and where it goes.

choices.label: Go Heavy on Posters & Banners (Traditional)
choices.description: Invest 60% of budget in high-quality printed posters and banners. Cover every corridor, every notice board, every stairwell. When students walk through school, they should see your face and message everywhere. The oldest campaign tactic in Indian politics.
choices.feedback:
Within three days, your posters blanket the school. Every corridor, every notice board, every stairwell. Students joke: 'I cannot go to the washroom without seeing your face.' Visibility is through the roof. But Ankit points out that poster-heavy campaigns generate awareness, not trust. 'I can see your face everywhere but I still do not know your policies,' a Class 10 student tells Priya. And Dr. Sharma raises an eyebrow at the printing costs on your expense report.

Did you know? In Indian elections, the ECI regulates campaign advertising and has the power to order removal of illegal hoardings. Political poster culture is deeply embedded in Indian democracy -- from hand-painted walls in villages to flex banners in cities. But the ECI increasingly monitors spending on such materials.

choices.label: Go Digital: Instagram, WhatsApp, and Video
choices.description: Invest in creating shareable content -- short reels, infographics, a campaign WhatsApp channel, and a polished manifesto PDF. Target the senior students who are always on their phones. Modern campaigning for a modern electorate.
choices.feedback:
Your Instagram campaign page hits 800 followers in a week. The WhatsApp manifesto PDF is forwarded across every class group. Your campaign reels get shared by students who would never attend a rally. Media coverage soars. But there is a problem: the Class 9 students -- your biggest potential vote bank -- barely use Instagram. They are on YouTube and offline. And the hostel students have limited phone access after 8 PM. Digital reached the seniors but missed the juniors.

Did you know? India has over 800 million internet users, making digital campaigning crucial. In the 2019 elections, the BJP's IT cell ran one of the world's most sophisticated digital campaigns. But critics point out that digital reach does not equal democratic participation -- millions of rural and lower-income voters remain offline.

choices.label: Invest in Events & Rallies
choices.description: Put your money into memorable campaign events -- a town hall with Q&A, a cultural evening where students perform, and a big pre-election rally. Face-to-face engagement creates the strongest emotional connections. This is the nukkad sabha of school politics.
choices.feedback:
Your town hall draws 300 students -- the best turnout for any candidate event. The cultural evening, where students perform and you speak between acts, creates genuine warmth. The rally has energy that no Instagram reel can replicate. Students who were undecided start leaning your way. But the events burned through your budget fast. Priya calculates: 'We have enough for two more weeks. After that, we are running on fumes.' The events were powerful, but expensive.

Did you know? Indian election rallies are legendary for their scale. A single rally can cost crores of rupees. The 'nukkad sabha' (street corner meeting) remains a cost-effective alternative that smaller parties and candidates use. The AAP's 2015 Delhi campaign was built on thousands of small mohalla sabhas rather than giant rallies.

choices.label: Chai Stalls & Ground Game (Grassroots)
choices.description: Set up chai stalls in different wings during breaks. Buy tea and biscuits, sit with students, listen to their problems over a cup of chai. No posters, no Instagram -- just real conversations. The cheapest and most personal approach. This is how elections are won in Indian villages.
choices.feedback:
Monday: chai stall outside the hostel. Tuesday: chai stall near the sports ground. Wednesday: chai stall in the science block corridor. By Thursday, students are actively seeking out your chai stall to share their problems. A senior tells you about ragging. A junior talks about not being able to afford the school trip. rounds.title: Round 10: Election Day
rounds.story:
The day has arrived. Voting booths are set up in the school library, supervised by Dr. Sharma and the election committee. Paper ballots -- just like real Indian elections. The NOTA option is on the ballot too, just as the Supreme Court mandated in 2013.

Dr. Sharma addresses the morning assembly: 'This is your democracy. Your vote is your voice. The ballot is secret. No one can know who you voted for. And remember -- after today, regardless of who wins, you are all students of Sardar Patel Vidyalaya. This school is bigger than any election.'

Voting is from 10 AM to 2 PM.

At 11 AM, Priya rushes up with alarming news: 'Turnout is low. Only 30% have voted so far, mostly Rohit's core supporters from the senior wings. Our voters -- the juniors, the hostel students, the quiet ones -- have not shown up yet. If this continues, we lose.'

She looks at you. 'We have three hours. What do we do?'

Meanwhile, Rohit's team is distributing free pens near the voting area -- technically a violation of the Model Code of Conduct.

rounds.goal: Maximise voter turnout on election day while maintaining integrity
rounds.setting: Election day -- school library voting booths, three hours remaining

npc_dialogue.text: The Model Code of Conduct prohibits campaigning near polling booths. No gifts, no pamphlets, no promises within the restricted zone. Any violation will be treated as it would be by the real Election Commission.
NOTA is on the ballot. If enough students are disillusioned, they will press NOTA instead of voting for anyone. We need to give them a reason to choose us, not just reject everyone.

choices.label: Personal Outreach: Visit Every Classroom and Hostel
choices.description: Mobilise your entire volunteer team for a final push. Personally visit every classroom, hostel room, and sports ground. Say: 'Please vote. Not for me -- just VOTE. Your voice matters.' Make it about democracy, not your candidacy. The padyatra approach, one last time.
choices.feedback:
You and your volunteers split up and cover the entire school. At the boys' hostel, you find 40 students watching cricket on TV. 'Three candidates fought for a month to earn your vote. Please spend two minutes telling us what you think.' One by one, they walk to the library. At the Junior Wing, your Class 9 volunteers personally escort friends to the booth. By 1:30 PM, turnout hits 78% -- the highest in school history. You may or may not win, but you strengthened democracy itself. Dr. Sharma nods approvingly: 'That is what democratic participation looks like.'

Did you know? India's Election Commission runs the SVEEP (Systematic Voters' Education and Electoral Participation) programme specifically to increase voter turnout. In the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, the ECI deployed lakhs of Booth Level Officers (BLOs) to motivate voters. Voter turnout is not just a statistic -- it is the health indicator of democracy. India's average turnout of ~67% in general elections compares to just 60% in the USA.

choices.label: Report Rohit's Free Pen Scheme to Dr. Sharma
choices.description: Rohit's free pen distribution near the polling area is a clear violation of the Model Code of Conduct. Report it formally and demand it be shut down. Uphold the rules. In a democracy, fair process matters as much as the outcome.
choices.feedback:
You file a formal complaint. Dr. Sharma investigates, confirms the violation, and shuts down Rohit's pen distribution at noon. Rohit receives a formal warning that will be announced with the results. His supporters are annoyed: 'It was just pens! Why are you being a buzzkill?' But Mr. Reddy, the Social Science teacher, quietly tells you: 'You did the right thing. Fair elections matter more than winning.' The pen booth closure reduces Rohit's advantage, but reinforces the perception that you are a 'complainer.' Principled, but not universally popular.

Did you know? The Election Commission of India has sweeping powers to ensure fair elections. It can postpone polls, countermand results, and disqualify candidates. In the 2019 elections alone, the ECI seized over Rs 3,400 crore worth of cash, liquor, drugs, and freebies meant to influence voters. The Model Code of Conduct is not just guidelines -- it is the backbone of electoral integrity in India.

choices.label: Request a Final 2-Minute PA System Appeal
choices.description: Ask Dr. Sharma for permission to make a brief appeal over the PA system during lunch break. Two minutes to reach every student in the school simultaneously. Your final words before the votes are cast.
choices.feedback:
Dr. Sharma grants every candidate two minutes on the PA. Rohit goes first -- polished promises. Then you: 'I am not the most popular candidate. I do not have the most money. But I have talked to more students in this school than anyone. I know the Class 9 students want the water cooler fixed. I know the hostel students want better food. I know the Class 12 students need exam support. I did not read this in a survey. I heard it from YOUR mouths. If that matters to you, please vote today.' The PA goes silent. Then corridors fill with students walking to the library. Turnout spikes in the final hour.

Did you know? The Election Commission enforces a 48-hour 'silence period' before polling in Indian elections -- no campaigning, no rallies, no appeals. This is meant to give voters time for calm reflection. In school elections, this translates to election day itself being a day of quiet democratic choice. The silence period is unique to Indian electoral law and is considered one of the ECI's most important innovations.

choices.label: Do Nothing: Trust the Campaign and the Voters
choices.description: You have campaigned for three weeks. Every handshake, every speech, every chai stall -- it is all done. On election day, trust the process. Sit in the canteen, have chai with Priya, and let the voters decide. Sometimes the most powerful thing a leader can do is step back.
choices.feedback:
You sit in the canteen with Priya, drinking chai. Your volunteers are nervous, asking: 'Should we not DO something?' But you say: 'We have done everything we can. Now it is their choice.' Ankit stops by and asks why you are not out mobilising. You say: 'Because democracy is about the voters, not the candidate. I trust them.' Ankit quotes you in his election day story. It is a dignified, mature stance. The question is whether dignity alone can overcome Rohit's aggressive final push.

Did you know? After voting ends in Indian elections, a period of 'counting' follows -- often days later. Candidates and their agents wait anxiously as EVMs (Electronic Voting Machines) are counted round by round. The suspense of Indian election results is legendary. Whether you actively campaign on election day or trust the process, the voters have the final word. That is the beauty of democracy.

How you behave when you know the result is uncertain tells voters who you'll be when you win. Getting out your genuine supporters matters far more than suppressing your opponent's.

endings.message: The votes are counted. Dr. Sharma reads the results in the packed auditorium. Your name echoes as students erupt in thunderous applause. You won with {{voter_support}}% voter support -- the highest margin in school history! Your campaign of authenticity, integrity, and genuine grassroots connection triumphed over Rohit's money and machinery. Even Rohit shakes your hand: 'You earned it.' As you step to the microphone, you see Priya, your junior volunteers, and the hostel students who believed in you. They are crying. You are crying. If three more juniors had stayed in their rooms instead of voting, you would have lost. This is the most powerful lesson of democracy: never assume your voice does not count. Come back stronger next year.' He is right. Defeat is not the end -- it is data. You now know more about leadership, ethics, democracy, and yourself than any textbook could teach. In Indian democracy, losing gracefully is as important as winning fairly. The campaign is over. The learning has just begun.

glossary_terms.definition: A public declaration of a candidate's or party's policies, promises, and vision for governance. In Indian elections, manifestos are released before polling and serve as a contract between the candidate and voters. The Supreme Court of India has discussed whether manifesto promises should be legally binding.
glossary_terms.example: The BJP's 2014 manifesto promised 'Minimum Government, Maximum Governance' and specific policy goals like Swachh Bharat and Make in India. In your school election, your manifesto details your plans for the canteen, grievance cell, and hostel reform.

glossary_terms.definition: An alliance of two or more political parties or groups that agree to work together, usually to form a government or win an election. In Indian politics, coalitions have been central since 1989 -- the NDA, UPA, and Third Front are all coalition formations. Coalitions require compromise and power-sharing.
glossary_terms.example: When the Hostel Students' Union allied with your campaign in exchange for prioritising food reform, that was coalition politics -- gaining strength through alliance at the cost of flexibility.

glossary_terms.definition: A survey conducted immediately after voters have cast their ballots, asking them which candidate they voted for. Exit polls are used to predict election results before official counting. In India, the Election Commission restricts the publication of exit polls until after the last phase of voting to prevent influencing voters in later phases.
glossary_terms.example: On election day at school, Ankit conducts an informal exit poll by asking students outside the library who they voted for. The results help predict the winner before the official count.

glossary_terms.definition: A set of guidelines issued by the Election Commission of India that governs the behaviour of political parties, candidates, and the government during elections. It covers speeches, processions, polling day behaviour, and the use of government machinery. Violations can lead to censure, FIRs, and even disqualification. The MCC comes into effect from the date of election announcement until results are declared.
glossary_terms.example: Rohit's distribution of free pens near the voting booth violated the Model Code of Conduct, just as distributing cash, liquor, or gifts to voters violates the MCC in real Indian elections. Dr. Sharma enforced the school's MCC with the same seriousness as the ECI.

glossary_terms.definition: An option on Indian ballot papers and EVMs that allows voters to officially reject all candidates without spoiling their ballot. NOTA was introduced following the Supreme Court's landmark judgment in PUCL v. Union of India (2013). While NOTA votes are counted, they do not affect the result -- the candidate with the most votes still wins even if NOTA gets more. It is a tool for voters to express dissatisfaction with all available choices.
glossary_terms.example: In your school election, the NOTA option is on the ballot. If students are disillusioned with both you and Rohit, they can choose NOTA to send a message that neither candidate earned their trust.
